newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House report questions military readiness.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House report questions military readiness.

text.p: The United States is no longer prepared for a military conflict like the 1991 Gulf War, the chairman of the House of Representatives National Security Committee said on Wednesday.

"The reality is that years of declining defence budgets, a smaller force structure, fewer personnel and ageing equipment coupled with an increase in the number of peacekeeping and humanitarian operations are stretching U.S. military forces to the breaking point," Representative Floyd Spence, a South Carolina Republican, said in a report on U.S. military readiness.
A Defence Department official, who asked not to be identified, rejected Spence's conclusions. "We have no evidence that there has been any dramatic reduction in readiness," he said.
The Pentagon is making its own quadrennial review of U.S. military capabilities.
Spence said he and committee staff members visited more than two dozen bases and over 50 units in the United States and Europe over the past seven months to prepare the report.
He said they found that members of all the military services were forced to work harder and longer to accomplish their missions because of budget and personnel cutbacks.
"Doing more with less may be the military's new motto, but it is not a sustainable strategy nor is it conductive to ensuring the long term preparedness of an all-volunteer force," he said.
Spence said training was being compromised and military equipment was ageing prematurely because of extended use.

He said the quality of military life for servicemen and women and their families was also being adversely affected, with two-thirds of military housing classified as inadequate and increased family separations. Because of this, many experienced members of the military were leaving the services.

"Taken together, these readiness problems will continue to seriously erode the preparedness of U.S. armed forces. The already destructive mismatches between strategy, forces and resources are worsening."

As an example of the problem, Spence said 125 Army infantry squads have no personnel assigned to them, equal to a full division of troops. He said in some squadrons parts were being taken off usable aircraft to keep others flying.

The Pentagon official responded that "While the anecdotal evidence that is presented in the report clearly in a micro-sense raises a red flag, as do the people that provided those quotes to the Spence report, I think it misses the boat in a macro-sense. There are no units that are reporting a dramatic drop in readiness."

The U.S. military is supposed to be able to fight two regional conflicts at the same time if necessary. U.S. units have been used for peacekeeping duties in Bosnia and Haiti in recent years, taking them away from combat training.
